B3C1.q: According to the Foreword, why does God exercise 'perfect dominion' over the things He has made?
options: Because He created them by natural necessity rather than by will
Because in making them He needed neither the help of an extrinsic agent nor pre-existing matter, being the universal efficient cause of all being
Because He alone among the gods possesses free will
Because His dominion is limited only to intelligent creatures
B3C1.explanation: Aquinas argues God's dominion is perfect because in creating He required no external help and no matter to work with, being the universal efficient cause of all being.

B3C1.q: How, according to this chapter, do intelligent creatures relate to divine government differently from non-intelligent things?
options: Intelligent creatures are excluded from divine government entirely
Intelligent creatures direct themselves to their end by their own actions, while non-intelligent things are directed by another
Non-intelligent things direct themselves while intelligent creatures are wholly passive
There is no difference; all creatures are governed identically
B3C1.explanation: The text states that intelligent beings 'bear a resemblance to Him' and so direct themselves to their end by their own actions, whereas things lacking intelligence are directed by another.

B3C1.q: How does the Foreword distinguish the subject matter of Book Three from that of Books One and Two?
options: Book Three treats God's perfect authority as the end and governor of all things, whereas Book One treated the divine nature and Book Two the divine power as creator and lord
Book Three repeats the arguments of Book One about the divine essence
Book Three is devoted solely to angelology
Book Three treats only the moral life of Christians, unrelated to the earlier books
B3C1.explanation: Aquinas explains that having treated the perfection of the divine nature (Bk I) and of the divine power as creator and lord (Bk II), Book Three treats God's perfection as end and governor of all things.

B3C2.q: Why, for Aquinas, must every agent's action tend toward something determinate rather than proceeding indefinitely?
options: Because an infinite series of actions could never begin, since an infinite medium cannot be passed through
Because God directly forbids indefinite action
Because matter is finite in quantity
Because only rational agents can act at all
B3C2.explanation: Aquinas argues that if an agent's action proceeded to infinity it could never begin to act, since it is impossible to pass through an infinite medium; hence every agent must tend to a determinate end.

B3C2.q: How does Aquinas explain that even non-intelligent natural agents 'intend' an end, such as fire generating fire?
options: Natural agents have no direction to an end at all, unlike intelligent agents
Just as the intellect preconceives its effect, the natural agent contains a similitude of its effect by which its action is determined to that effect
Natural agents act purely by chance
Natural agents borrow their intention from an external observer
B3C2.explanation: Aquinas draws a parallel: as the intellect preconceives the effect it aims at, so in the natural agent there pre-exists a likeness of its natural effect that determines its action toward that end.

B3C2.q: How does Aquinas handle apparently purposeless actions like idly scratching one's beard, as an objection to 'every agent acts for an end'?
options: He admits such actions prove some agents act for no end at all
He says these actions arise from imagination or a natural cause rather than intellect, yet still tend toward some end outside the order of intellect
He denies that such actions actually occur
He claims such actions are miracles
B3C2.explanation: Aquinas explains that unattended actions like scratching one's beard proceed from a sudden imaginative impulse or bodily cause rather than deliberate intellect, but they still tend to an end, just outside the intellect's ordering.

B3C3.q: What is the central conclusion Aquinas draws in this chapter about every agent's action?
options: Every agent acts for a good, since what an agent tends to definitely must be befitting to it, and what is befitting is good
Every agent acts randomly without any orientation toward good or evil
Only rational agents act for a good; natural agents act for neither good nor evil
Agents act for evil more often than for good
B3C3.explanation: Aquinas concludes every agent acts for a good, since an agent's definite tendency toward something implies fittingness to that agent, and what is fitting is good.

B3C3.q: Which classical definition of 'good' does Aquinas invoke to support his argument in this chapter?
options: Good is whatever is pleasurable to the senses
The good is the object of every appetite
Good is simply the absence of pain
Good is whatever the majority desires
B3C3.explanation: Aquinas cites the philosophers' definition, 'the good is the object of every appetite,' and Dionysius's statement that all things desire the good and the best.

B3C3.q: How does Aquinas explain that a natural agent (which lacks intellect) still acts 'for a good' even though it does not grasp the notion of 'end' as such?
options: A natural agent's end is determined for it by an appetite oriented toward a good, even without conceptual knowledge of that end as an end
Natural agents have no genuine end whatsoever
Natural agents borrow their goal from human observers who assign it a purpose
Natural agents act for evil unless corrected by an intellectual agent
B3C3.explanation: Aquinas notes that while an intellectual agent determines its end under the aspect of good known as such, a natural agent is moved toward an end that is a good, determined for it by its appetite, without cognizing the ratio of end.

B3C4.q: What is the main thesis Aquinas establishes in this chapter regarding evil?
options: Evil is always intended directly by some agent
Evil occurs beside (outside) the intention of every agent, since every agent intends a good
Evil has no cause of any kind
Evil and good are intended equally by every agent
B3C4.explanation: Since every agent intends a good, and evil differs from good, Aquinas concludes evil results beside the intention of the agent, i.e., unintentionally.

B3C4.q: In the example of matter and form used in this chapter, why does the corruption of a prior form (e.g., air, when fire is generated) happen unintentionally?
options: Because matter intends the privation of the old form for its own sake
Because matter's appetite and tendency is toward the new form, and the privation of the old form is a necessary but unintended consequence
Because matter has no potentiality for any form
Because privation is impossible according to Aquinas
B3C4.explanation: Aquinas explains matter tends per se toward the form it is acquiring (e.g., fire), and the privation of the prior form (air) is an unintended, accidental result of attaining that form.

B3C4.q: What analogy does Aquinas use to explain how an intellectual agent can do evil unintentionally?
options: Mistaking gall for honey while intending to eat honey
A gardener accidentally watering weeds
A sculptor breaking a statue by accident
A blind man walking into a wall
B3C4.explanation: Aquinas compares committing evil unintentionally to a man who intends to eat honey but eats gall thinking it is honey; the evil result is beside his intention, since he acted under the appearance of a good.

B3C5.q: What objection does this chapter raise against the claim that 'evil is beside the intention'?
options: That evil occurs so rarely it cannot be beside intention
That evil (like corruption following generation, or frequent sin) occurs always or frequently, not rarely as 'beside intention' implies, and that Aristotle calls vice voluntary
That Aristotle denies evil exists at all
That evil is identical with matter
B3C5.explanation: The objection notes that what is beside an agent's intention is typically called fortuitous and rare, yet evil (corruption, sin) occurs constantly, and Aristotle explicitly calls vice voluntary, seemingly contradicting the 'beside intention' thesis.

B3C5.q: How does Aquinas resolve the objection that what is 'unintentional' should be rare, while evil (like natural corruption) occurs constantly?
options: He denies that corruption is really evil
He distinguishes: what is unintentional can still follow necessarily and constantly from what is intended, so it is not thereby 'casual' or rare
He argues corruption is intended directly by nature for its own sake
He claims the objection is entirely correct and abandons his earlier thesis
B3C5.explanation: Aquinas explains that something unintended can nonetheless occur constantly if it necessarily accompanies what is directly intended (e.g., getting drunk when one intends only to enjoy wine); such regularity does not make it intended per se.

B3C5.q: In this chapter, how is moral evil (such as adultery) said to be voluntary even though it is not intended per se?
options: It is not voluntary at all, contrary to Aristotle
The will intends the pleasurable good sought, and wills the accompanying disorder only 'for the sake of' that good, similar to throwing cargo overboard for safety
Moral evil is always intended for its own sake as the final end
Moral evil results purely from ignorance and thus involves no will at all
B3C5.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of jettisoning cargo to save a ship: one does not intend the loss simply, but wills it for the sake of something else; likewise the sinner wills the disordered act for the sake of the sensible good sought, not for its own sake.

B3C6.q: This chapter (largely repeating and extending Chapter 5's material) distinguishes evil 'simply' from evil 'of a particular thing.' What example does it give of something lacking that is NOT an evil simply?
options: A man lacking wings, since it is not natural for him to have them
A man lacking a hand, since hands are natural and due to a perfect human being
A bird lacking feathers
A fish lacking the form of water
B3C6.explanation: The text explains that a man's lacking wings is no evil to him because wings are not natural or due to him, unlike lacking a hand, which is an evil since a hand is natural and due to a complete human being.

B3C6.q: According to the solution given here, why is the privation of the form of air (e.g., when fire is generated) not an 'evil simply'?
options: Because privation of form is never an evil in any sense
Because it is only an evil relative to air (the thing losing its form), not an evil simply, since matter as such is not owed any one particular form
Because air has no matter
Because generation of fire is itself sinful
B3C6.explanation: The text distinguishes privation relative to the subject that loses something due to it (evil simply) from privation merely relative to matter in general, which is due no specific form; hence loss of air's form is only 'an evil of the air,' not evil simply.

B3C6.q: How does the chapter explain that nature does not, strictly speaking, intend the corruption (e.g., of water) that accompanies generation (e.g., of air)?
options: Nature intends corruption and generation equally and directly as two separate goals
Nature directly intends the new form (e.g., air) to exist; the exclusion of the old form (water) follows only because the two cannot coexist, so privation is intended only accidentally
Nature intends nothing at all in physical processes
Nature intends only the destruction of forms, never their generation
B3C6.explanation: The text states nature's direct intention is that air should exist; since air's existence precludes water's, the privation of water follows only accidentally, not because nature directly intends non-being.

B3C7.q: What is the main conclusion of this chapter regarding the nature of evil?
options: Evil is a positive essence created directly by God
No essence is evil in itself, since evil is merely the privation of what is connatural and due to a thing
Evil and good are equally real substances
Only immaterial things can be evil
B3C7.explanation: Aquinas concludes that evil is not a real essence but the privation of what is connatural and due to a subject; hence nothing is evil simply by virtue of having an essence.

B3C7.q: Why does Aquinas say that 'in so far as a thing has an essence, it is good'?
options: Because essence and evil are synonymous in his system
Because to have being is to be an object of desire (since all things desire being), and thus being as such shares in goodness
Because only rational essences can be good
Because Aquinas equates essence with pleasure
B3C7.explanation: Since good is what all things desire, and all things desire being, Aquinas concludes that being itself, and therefore having an essence, is good; evil and good being opposites, nothing is evil simply by having an essence.

B3C7.q: Whose position does Aquinas explicitly refute at the end of this chapter by denying that any essence is evil in itself?
options: The Pelagians
The Manichees, who held that some things are evil by their very nature
The Stoics
The Nestorians
B3C7.explanation: Aquinas closes by refuting the Manichean error, which held that certain things are evil by their very nature, i.e., that evil has a positive essence.

B3C8.q: One objection in this chapter argues evil must be a real 'thing' because it functions as a specific difference (e.g., distinguishing vice from virtue). How does Aquinas resolve this?
options: He agrees evil is a positive essence in moral matters only

He explains that in morals, 'evil' names an end that is good in itself (e.g., a sensible pleasure) but discordant with reason, so it does not denote something evil in essence but a privation of right order to reason
He denies vice and virtue differ in species at all
He claims moral evil is purely imaginary and has no real effects
B3C8.explanation: Aquinas explains that the object called 'evil' in a moral species (e.g., an inordinate pleasure) is actually good in itself; it is termed evil only because it lacks conformity to reason's due order, so evil remains a privation, not a positive nature.

B3C8.q: How does Aquinas address the objection that evil must be 'active' since it corrupts and counteracts good?
options: He denies evil ever corrupts anything

He explains evil is not a principle of action by itself; it 'corrupts' only by virtue of the good it is joined to, and formally as a privation, similar to how blindness 'corrupts' sight by being its very absence
He claims evil is a stronger active force than good
He says corruption is always caused directly by God
B3C8.explanation: Citing Dionysius, Aquinas argues evil is powerless and weak, acting (accidentally) only by virtue of some good; it 'corrupts' formally as blindness corrupts sight, being the very privation of it, not an active power in itself.

B3C8.q: How does Aquinas explain that one evil can be called 'greater' than another, given that evil is a mere privation and not a positive quality admitting degrees?
options: Degrees of evil are illusions with no basis in reality
A thing is called a greater evil by reason of greater distance from the good, and privations increase through the increase of their cause, not through evil possessing its own essence
Evil has its own essence that can literally increase, like heat
There are no degrees of evil according to Aquinas
B3C8.explanation: Aquinas explains that greater evil means greater distance from good; privation admits degrees through the increasing cause of the privation (e.g., more obstacles blocking light), not because privation itself is a graduated essence.

B3C9.q: This chapter (paralleling Chapter 8) addresses the objection that 'good and evil' are called genera of contraries by Aristotle, which would seem to make evil a nature. How does Aquinas explain this Aristotelian claim?
options: Aristotle asserts this as his own settled doctrine that evil is a positive nature
Aquinas suggests Aristotle is reporting Pythagoras's opinion (which listed evil among ten supreme contraries) as a probable view current among other philosophers, not asserting evil has true essence
Aristotle never discusses good and evil as genera anywhere
This claim is a later medieval forgery unrelated to Aristotle
B3C9.explanation: Aquinas notes Aristotle may be presenting the Pythagorean scheme of ten paired contraries (including good and evil) as a probable opinion of others, in his logical works, rather than asserting evil is truly a genus or essence.

B3C9.q: According to this chapter, in what sense do 'good and evil' relate to the imperfect and perfect members of any pair of contraries (e.g., hot/cold, white/black)?
options: Both members of every contrary pair are equally perfect and equally good
One contrary is perfect (associated with good) while the other involves some privation (associated with evil), since incompleteness is a kind of evil and completeness a kind of good
Contraries have no relation whatsoever to good and evil
All contraries are evil without exception
B3C9.explanation: The text explains that of any pair of contraries, one is complete/perfect (e.g., white, hot) and thus akin to good, while the other involves privation (e.g., black, cold) and thus approaches the notion of evil.

B3C9.q: How does this chapter explain the claim that 'evil exists in the world,' given that evil has no essence?
options: It denies evil exists in the world in any sense

Evil is said to 'be' only in the sense of a true predication that a subject is deprived by a privation (the 'is' of synthetic truth), not in the sense of belonging to one of the ten categories of substantial being
It affirms evil is a full category of being alongside the other nine categories
Evil's existence is purely a matter of human opinion with no truth value
B3C9.explanation: Following Aristotle's distinction, Aquinas explains 'being' predicated as truth (a subject truly is deprived) differs from being predicated as essence (the ten categories); evil 'exists' only in the first, propositional sense.

B3C10.q: What is the central claim of this chapter regarding the cause of evil?
options: Evil is uncaused and simply happens spontaneously
Evil is never caused by anything, not even accidentally
Evil is caused only accidentally, and always by some good, since evil itself (being non-being) cannot be a per se cause of anything
Evil is caused directly and intentionally by good agents
B3C10.explanation: Aquinas argues that because evil is not a being, it cannot be a cause per se; whatever causes evil must be traced back to some good acting as an accidental, deficient cause.

B3C10.q: How does Aquinas explain evil arising 'on the part of the agent' in physical processes, such as imperfect digestion?
options: The agent intentionally chooses to produce a defective effect
A defect in the agent's power (not the agent's power as such) results in a deficient effect; the cause is called 'deficient' rather than truly 'efficient' with respect to that defect
Evil in this case has no relation to the agent's causal power at all
Digestion is a moral rather than physical process
B3C10.explanation: Aquinas explains that when an agent's power is defective, the resulting deficient action or effect (like imperfect digestion) follows accidentally from that defect, so the defective power is called a 'deficient,' not truly 'efficient,' cause of the evil.

B3C10.q: In tracing moral fault to its root, which of the four principles of moral action (apprehended object, apprehensive power, will, executive/motive power) does Aquinas identify as where moral fault is properly first found?
options: The executive or motive power that moves the bodily members
The apprehended object itself
The act of the will, since morality depends on what is voluntary
The apprehensive power's judgment alone, prior to any act of will
B3C10.explanation: Aquinas argues that defects in the executive power or the apprehensive power excuse or diminish fault (like ignorance or weakness), so moral fault is found first and chiefly in the act of the will, since an act is 'moral' precisely because voluntary.

B3C11.q: What does this chapter conclude about the 'subject' in which evil is seated?
options: Evil exists without any subject, floating free
Every evil is seated in some good, since evil (a privation) requires a subject, and every subject as a substance is itself good
Evil is seated only in other evils, forming an infinite regress
Evil has no subject because it does not truly exist at all
B3C11.explanation: Aquinas argues that since evil has no essence of its own, it must exist in some subject, and since every subject, as a being, is good, it follows that every evil is seated in some good.

B3C11.q: How does Aquinas resolve the apparent paradox that good and evil are opposites, yet good is said to be the 'subject' of evil?
options: He denies good and evil are really opposed to each other

He explains that evil is not seated in its own opposite good (the very good it deprives) but in some other good, e.g., moral evil is in a natural good, and privation of form is in matter as a good in potentiality
He claims evil and good are actually identical in reality
He argues only immaterial substances can be subjects of evil
B3C11.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that evil is not seated in the specific good it excludes (as blindness is not 'in' sight) but in some other underlying good, such as an animal (for blindness) or matter as a potential being (for privation of form).

B3C11.q: What example does Aquinas use to illustrate that privation (like blindness) has being as its subject without being 'in' the being it directly opposes?
options: Blindness is in the eye's sight, which it destroys
Blindness is not universal non-being but a particular privation of sight, and so is seated in the animal, not in sight itself
Blindness is not a privation at all but a positive quality
Blindness exists independently of any living subject
B3C11.explanation: Aquinas explains blindness is a particular non-being (privation of sight specifically), and its subject is the animal that lacks sight, not sight itself, since sight and its privation cannot coexist in the same respect.

B3C12.q: What is the main thesis of this chapter about evil's capacity to destroy good?
options: Evil can and eventually will destroy all good entirely, given enough time
However much evil increases, it can never entirely destroy good, because the subject of evil, which is itself a good, must always remain as long as the evil exists
Good and evil destroy each other simultaneously and completely
Evil destroys good only in moral matters, never in physical nature
B3C12.explanation: Aquinas argues that since evil must have some good as its subject, that subject-good can never be totally annihilated by the evil that resides in it; evil diminishes but cannot wholly eliminate the underlying good.

B3C12.q: How does Aquinas explain that good is 'diminished' by evil, rather than by literal subtraction of good's quantity?
options: Good is diminished only by removing physical parts of the subject
Good is diminished more by the addition of a contrary actuality that blocks the subject's potentiality to the good, similar to how increasing heat in a subject makes it less potentially cold
Good cannot be diminished at all, only destroyed outright
Evil adds a positive quantity that literally replaces the good's substance
B3C12.explanation: Aquinas explains diminishment happens because a contrary actuality (the evil) increasingly blocks the subject's potentiality toward the excluded good, rather than good literally losing 'parts,' using the analogy of heat progressively excluding a subject's potential coldness.

B3C12.q: Why, according to this chapter, can moral evil diminish the good of nature indefinitely, in a way physical evil cannot diminish physical good indefinitely?
options: Because physical forms and forces are limited and reach fixed terms, whereas intellect and will have no fixed limit, so vice can be indefinitely repeated and entrenched
Because moral evil is not really evil at all
Because physical evil is always worse than moral evil
Because the will has a naturally fixed, unchangeable capacity for evil that cannot increase
B3C12.explanation: Aquinas notes physical forms/forces are limited and reach a maximum, but intellect and will can proceed indefinitely (e.g., repeated theft), so moral evil can diminish the good of nature indefinitely without ever wholly destroying it.

B3C13.q: What does this chapter establish about whether evil has any cause at all?
options: Evil has no cause whatsoever, per se or accidental
Although evil has no per se cause, every evil must nonetheless have some accidental cause, since it exists in a good subject and represents potentiality actuated toward a defect
Evil is its own cause, being self-generating
Only moral evil has a cause; physical evil is uncaused
B3C13.explanation: Aquinas argues that since evil resides in a good subject and represents a potentiality toward defect that must be actuated by something, evil must have some cause, even though it cannot be a per se cause of anything.

B3C13.q: Why does Aquinas say a stone is not naturally borne upward, and water not naturally heated, unless 'something else' causes it — and how does this support his argument about evil?
options: This example is irrelevant to the discussion of evil's cause

Because whatever is beyond a thing's nature (like upward motion for a stone, or evil for a good subject) requires an external cause, supporting the claim that evil, being contrary to a subject's nature, must have a cause
Because stones and water have no nature at all
Because this proves natural motion is always evil
B3C13.explanation: Aquinas uses the example to show that whatever exceeds or departs from a thing's own nature (like a stone moving up, or evil being present in a naturally good subject) requires some other cause to bring it about.

B3C14.q: What is the central claim of this chapter regarding evil as a cause?
options: Evil is a per se cause of many good effects

Although evil is not a per se cause, it is nevertheless an accidental cause of things, in the same way something accidental to a per se cause (like whiteness to a builder) can be called an accidental cause of the builder's product
Evil cannot be any kind of cause under any description
Evil is the only true cause of anything, while good causes nothing
B3C14.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of a builder who happens to be white: whiteness is an accidental cause of the house because it is accidental to the per se cause (the builder); similarly evil, being seated in a good that is a per se cause, becomes an accidental cause.

B3C14.q: How does Aquinas show that evil functions as an accidental cause across all four Aristotelian causes (efficient, material, formal, final)?
options: He shows evil functions only as a final cause, never the others
In each case, defect in some good factor (deficient efficient power, indisposed matter, privation accompanying form, or hindrance to the due end) accidentally results in a defective effect
He argues evil can never be linked to material or formal causation, only efficient
He denies evil relates to causation in any of the four kinds
B3C14.explanation: Aquinas surveys efficient (defective agent), material (indisposed matter), formal (privation accompanying form), and final (hindering the due end) causes, showing evil enters accidentally into each without being a cause per se in any of them.

B3C15.q: What position does this chapter refute by arguing there can be no 'sovereign evil' or first principle of all evils?
options: The Pelagian heresy regarding grace
The error of the Manichees, who held there is a supreme evil as the first principle of all evils, opposed to a supreme good
The Arian denial of Christ's divinity
The Sabellian confusion of the Persons of the Trinity
B3C15.explanation: Aquinas explicitly closes the chapter by refuting the Manichean error, which posited a sovereign evil as an independent first principle parallel to the sovereign good.

B3C15.q: Why, according to Aquinas, can there be no evil that is 'essentially evil' in the way the supreme good is essentially good?
options: Because evil has no essence at all, whereas being essentially evil would require evil to have an essence
Because essence and evil are the same thing by definition
Because only the supreme good has any essence at all
Because created things can never possess any essence
B3C15.explanation: Since evil has already been shown to have no essence (Chapter 7), nothing can be 'essentially evil' the way the supreme good is essentially good; hence no supreme, self-subsisting evil is possible.

B3C15.q: What causal argument does Aquinas give for why evil cannot function as a 'first principle'?
options: Evil is caused by good and is only an accidental cause itself, whereas a genuine first principle would have to be uncaused and act by its own proper power
Evil is uncaused and therefore perfectly qualifies as a first principle
First principles must always be evil, by definition, according to Aquinas
Evil precedes good in the order of causality
B3C15.explanation: Since every evil is caused by a good and evil acts only accidentally (never by its own proper power as a per se, uncaused cause), it cannot fulfill the role of an uncaused first principle.
